layers.text: HOW A TOKEN INDEX GETS SMALL
one vector per document, or one per token?
one vector for the whole text
one vector per token  ·  128 numbers each
late interaction: query and document meet only at the end
≈ 118 KB per document, before any compression
Pooling: merge tokens that point the same way
pool by 2 → ½ the vectors   ·   pool by 4 → ¼
Fewer bytes, a higher score  ·  SciFact
Let the quantizer set the pooling?
merge while merge error ≤ coding error
against uniform pooling at the same size (nDCG@10):
LateOn on SciFact and NFCorpus  ·  oaustegard/experiments, lateon-pool-remex

audio.text: Most search engines squeeze a document into one vector. [[col]][ColBERT](/kQlbˈɛə/) keeps one for every token. Here's how it scores, why that gets big, and how to make it [[small]]small.
audio.speaker: bm_fable,bm_fable,bm_lewis

audio.text: A single-vector model [[averages]]averages the whole text into one point. [[colb]][ColBERT](/kQlbˈɛə/) gives each token its own vector, a hundred and twenty-eight numbers long. So a specific word, like the D in vitamin D, keeps its own [[say]]say in the score.
audio.speaker: bm_fable,bm_fable,bm_lewis

audio.text: To score a document, each query token looks for its most similar document token. [[take]]Take that best match for every query token, and [[add]]add them up. That's max-sim: [[late]]late interaction, because query and document only meet at the end.
audio.speaker: bm_fable,bm_fable,bm_lewis

audio.text: The catch is size. [[lateon]]LateOn, a strong [ColBERT](/kQlbˈɛə/) model, keeps about two hundred and thirty vectors per document. At four bytes a number, that's [[kb]]a hundred and eighteen kilobytes, for every single document.
audio.speaker: bm_fable,bm_fable,bm_lewis

audio.text: There are [[two]]two ways to shrink it. [[fewer]]Keep fewer vectors. [[bits]]Or spend fewer bits on each one.
audio.speaker: bm_fable,bm_fable,bm_lewis

audio.text: Pooling merges tokens that point the same way. [[ward]]Ward clustering groups a document's tokens, and each group becomes its [[avg]]average. [[half]]Pool by two, and half the vectors remain. Pool by four, and a [[quarter]]quarter.
audio.speaker: bm_fable,bm_fable,bm_lewis

audio.text: Quantizing is [remex](/ɹˈiːmɛks/)'s job. [[cone]]LateOn's vectors crowd into a narrow cone, so [remex](/ɹˈiːmɛks/) first [[subtract]]subtracts their average. Then it [[rotate]]rotates them, and [[snap]]snaps every coordinate to a few levels: sixteen levels at four bits. Just [[one]]two at one bit.
audio.speaker: bm_fable,bm_fable,bm_lewis

audio.text: So which wins at a similar size? On SciFact, [[every]]every token at one bit takes five and a half kilobytes per document and scores point seven four nine. [[quarter]]A quarter of the tokens at four bits takes four point two kilobytes and scores point seven six oh: [[nearly]]nearly the full index, at under four percent of its size.
audio.speaker: bm_fable,bm_fable,bm_lewis

audio.text: We also let the quantizer decide how far to pool: merge until the merge error matches the coding error. [[free]]That's free at three and four bits. [[but]]But it didn't beat plain pooling. It won on one dataset, and [[lost]]lost on the other.
audio.speaker: bm_fable,bm_fable,bm_lewis

audio.text: So, for a token index: [[pool]]pool the tokens, [[keep]]keep at least two bits, and [[center]]center before you quantize.
audio.speaker: bm_fable,bm_fable,bm_lewis
